draft.title: Momentum of photons and matter
card: A photon has momentum even though it has no mass. Its momentum is p = h/λ, where λ is its wavelength and h is Planck's constant.
De Broglie proposed that a particle with momentum p has a wavelength λ = h/p. This is the same relation, written the other way round.
So a photon and a particle with the same wavelength have the same momentum. A shorter wavelength means a larger momentum.
The particle moves much more slowly than the photon. An electron with the same momentum as a photon still has a speed far below the speed of light.
draft.remember: Same wavelength means same momentum, p = h/λ, for photons and for particles.

a.q: An electron and a photon both have a wavelength of 0.20 nm. How do their momenta compare?
opts: They are equal
The electron's is larger
The photon's is larger
The photon's is zero, as it has no mass
a.why: Both follow p = h/λ, and λ and h are the same, so the momenta are equal. A photon has no mass, but it still has momentum.
a.clue: Use the same equation for both and compare the wavelengths.

b.q: A proton has the same momentum as an X-ray photon. Which statement about their wavelengths is correct?
opts: They are equal, since λ = h/p for both
The proton's is longer, since it has mass
The photon's is longer, since it moves faster
The proton's is shorter, since it is heavier
b.why: Wavelength is h divided by momentum, and the momentum is the same, so the wavelengths are equal. Mass and speed do not matter once the momentum is known.
b.clue: Wavelength depends only on h and momentum.

b.best: They are equal, since λ = h/p for both

problems.detail: The last bullet says an electron with the same momentum as a photon 'still has a speed far below the speed of light.' That is true for everyday wavelengths like 0.2 nm, but it is not true in general. An electron matched to a high-energy photon (for example, MeV gamma rays) moves at close to the speed of light. Limit it with 'typically' or 'at these wavelengths', or remove it.
The clue 'Wavelength depends only on h and momentum' effectively states the answer. It rules out every option that appeals to mass or speed.

check.summary: The card overstates that an electron with the same momentum as a photon always moves far below light speed. This is false at high momenta. Question b's clue also gives the answer away. Both answers (equal momenta, equal wavelengths) are correct.
